📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not the whole startup - just its tech and the brains behind it.
  • Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations.
  • The house of Bezos on Monday revealed a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not the whole startup - just its tech and the brains behind it.

Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations.

The house of Bezos on Monday revealed a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also looks to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold.

Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.”.

DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips.

Industry observers note that “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.”.

Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs.

An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full manufacturer acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back.

Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications.

Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion.

Industry observers note that if Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM. ®.

Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whatever they call themselves these days: be on the lookout for voice phishing attempts.
  • In a recent development, don't mind the recent arrests.
  • ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whatever they call themselves these days: be on the lookout for voice phishing attempts.

In a recent development, don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the upcoming name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group.

ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark.

“While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels remarked on Monday.

Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group.

While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA).

It has been revealed that plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters.

Recent findings suggest that the first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media.

On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims.

None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information.

Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions.

In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s upcoming data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.”.

The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added.

It has been revealed that the Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure.

In a recent development, “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot presently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.”.

Industry observers note that regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, great news from the OGs of open source LLMs!
  • To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries.
  • Recent findings suggest that scores are reported as published.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, great news from the OGs of open source LLMs! Muse Glimmer, released today, is Meta’s new multimodal model, especially designed for local agentic use cases. Distilled from Muse to 30B parameters, and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it’s ideal deploying locally for privacy, reducing costs, or just hacking around. It’s intended for privacy-aware applications such as coding, document analysis, personal assistants, Claw- or Hermes-like setups.

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Recent findings suggest that scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:.

Sources indicate that in addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

It has been revealed that after transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer comes with day-0 llama.cpp support. Meta has distributed calibrated quants in this repo, and Unsloth is releasing optimized quants as well. DFlash speculative decoding is supported as well. You can use a pre-built llama binary to start a llama server or a CLI. To install llama.cpp, run:.

In a recent development, DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

Below you can see how speculative decoding can speed-up generation in realistic setups. The video indicates llama.cpp webui with DFlash on the left and regular generation on the right.

In a recent development, you can start llama server using following command. --spec-draft-n-max argument controls how many future tokens DFlash proposes during each speculative-decoding step. Muse Glimmer’s DFlash model was trained with a block size of 16, one anchor token plus 15 proposed tokens, so any value above 15 will be clamped to 15.

Industry observers note that for a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

Sources indicate that the deployed model exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Keep your Hugging Face token in an environment variable, set HF_ENDPOINT_URL to the URL shown in the Overview without /v1, and set HF_ENDPOINT_MODEL to the endpoint's model name.

See the Inference Endpoints documentation for configuration, autoscaling, security, logs, and monitoring.

For this release, we ship support for vLLM with transformers backend.

In a recent development, you can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

Industry observers note that as part of this release, we ship an example to fine-tune Muse Glimmer on small split of MolmoWeb dataset. This demonstrates how to make model generate structured outputs and how to fine-tune on images.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀.

Assume the Inference Endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 API.

Set HF_TOKEN in the OpenClaw gateway environment, then add this to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:.

Use the exact model ID returned by the endpoint’s /v1/models response if it differs.

Recent findings suggest that if we hook up Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face MCP and update its AGENTS.md we give it the capability to find a quantized version of itself on the hub and run locally. This is handy if you want to work on something private, or just cut costs.

If you do this a second time, Muse Glimmer will find the cached weights and switch to them, so feel free to add a convenient command like /spawn.

Muse Glimmer inspects the machine and Hub, selects or creates a Q4_K_M GGUF, launches llama-server, and validates model discovery and chat completion. The result is a smaller local build behind an OpenAI-compatible API. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md.

Muse Glimmer can also take care of the opposite. Let’s get Glimmer to deploy itself on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints. Which is useful if you want to speed up on some cutting edge hardware.

Muse Glimmer pins the model revision, deploys it to a protected Hugging Face Inference Endpoint, and verifies health, model discovery, and chat completion. It then connects the Claw agent with secrets and rollback preserved. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer will also need the Hugging Face MCP and/or the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

Finally, let’s get Muse Glimmer to do some light RSI. We can instruct our agent to optimize its own inference engine for specific hardware, in this case a Nvidia H100. To do this, the agent will need to use another inference engine, like Inference Endpoints above.

Muse Glimmer benchmarks its own single-H100 serving stack, testing one reversible change at a time while holding the workload fixed. It keeps only correctness-passing gains and finishes with the fastest reproducible configuration. Here’s the prompt we added to AGENTS.md. Muse glimmer need the Hugging Face MCP and the Hugging Face CLI and Skills.

https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/muse-glimmer-assets/resolve/onyx-optimization-progress.gif?download=true.

Sources indicate that try Muse Glimmer as a Hugging Face research agent. The Gradio Space sends each model request to a private Hugging Face Inference Endpoint through its OpenAI-compatible API. It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

It has been revealed that we are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a Newly introduced Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer looks like a really exciting step for practical open-source AI, especially with its focus on local, agentic, and multimodal workloads. A 30B-parameter model combining a 2B vision encoder with a 28B text decoder gives developers a strong foundation for coding, document analysis, personal assistants, and other privacy-sensitive applications. 🔥🤖.

The Apache 2.0 license is another major highlight because it makes the model much more approachable for developers who want to experiment, customize, and deploy without relying entirely on hosted inference. Local deployment can also bring meaningful benefits around privacy, latency, and infrastructure costs, which makes this especially interesting for personal and enterprise workflows. 🚀.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

It has been revealed that the day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏.

Industry News: GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

In a recent development, that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

It has been revealed that the East US 3 buildout is about one week behind blueprint. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to enhancement, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Recent findings suggest that actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

Sources indicate that A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

Sources indicate that the importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Sources indicate that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or problems, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

It has been revealed that web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

In a recent development, during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

Industry observers note that an internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Sources indicate that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, latest connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Recent findings suggest that audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Sources indicate that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Upcoming requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

Recent findings suggest that the pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

According to recent reports, follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

Anthropic indicates Claude solved an age-old math problem, but the written proof is 250,000 pages of slop

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If the AI can't explain what it's proven, are we actually any closer to understanding?
  • The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe.
  • But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the AI can't explain what it's proven, are we actually any closer to understanding?

The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe.

But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box?

Industry observers note that that question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure.

In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so important that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them.

The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2.

Recent findings suggest that confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here. What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros. There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that.

Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate.

According to recent reports, the four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs.

The Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. For Clay to consider the problem solved and award the prize, the proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, remain available for scrutiny for at least two years, and receive broad acceptance from the mathematics community.

As it stands, Alpöge describes the 250,000 pages of text generated by the model for its written proof as a “massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop.’”.

Industry observers note that not long after Alpöge's remarks and Lean code were published, Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil released a nearly 1,000-page draft proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, who earned his PhD at Stanford in 2020. Masullo has reportedly spent more than a decade pursuing the problem.

Frameworks like Lean make mathematics a prime candidate for AI-assisted discovery for many of the same reasons that the technology has proven so successful in software development: code either compiles and runs or it doesn’t.

Code can also be audited and could, with great effort, be deciphered. But a proof written in Lean isn't a mathematical proof in the traditional, human-readable sense. Although its logical validity can be checked by a computer, understanding the reasoning behind it can be another matter. Traditional proofs ideally explain their arguments in a way that other mathematicians can follow. Cantor's Diagonal Argument offers a comparatively accessible example.

While the clock hasn’t even started for the Clay Math Institute, the Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative have already declared the Riemann Hypothesis solved.

According to recent reports, “We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the orgs wrote in a joint statement. “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.”.

Even if the code ends up being right, if we still don’t know why it’s true, have we really learned anything meaningful?

"At the minute, we don't even know why the theorem is true," Kevin Buzzard, professor of pure mathematics at Imperial College London, said in a recent Al Jazeera interview.

Industry observers note that alpöge’s proof may simply be the product of a black box. To quote the late Arthur C Clarke, “any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.”.

The implications of such a technology aren’t lost on researchers. Months ago, several prominent researchers called for greater scrutiny and oversight regarding the application of AI in mathematics.

“Mathematics produces not only a body of results, but also understanding, clarity, and judgment among the communities of mathematicians who have shaped them, often in the context of their own autonomously guided research,” the Leiden Declaration reads. “This expert knowledge is essential, both to effectively use mathematics, and to continue to articulate new and significant research questions.” ®.

Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

📅 10 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning.
  • The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline.
  • The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

In a recent development, as a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

In a recent development, dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Industry observers note that offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

According to recent reports, A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:.

The GIF below reveals the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

In a recent development, the loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only highlights up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

According to recent reports, to see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

It has been revealed that distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

According to recent reports, want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

Breaking: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ‘Shirudo’ project promises to whip up compensating controls in a hurry.
  • Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for owners who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws.
  • Industry observers note that shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘Shirudo’ project promises to whip up compensating controls in a hurry.

Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for owners who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws.

Industry observers note that shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources.

Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project.

Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders.

It has been revealed that the increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch.

With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things:.

The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux;.

Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed.

“Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production.

According to recent reports, shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation.

Recent findings suggest that cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls.

Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it.

Recent findings suggest that that offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that by the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response.
  • The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

Industry observers note that by the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:.

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:.

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (newly introduced) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new).

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before people hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most crucial latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

Industry observers note that the table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Recent findings suggest that because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Industry observers note that low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

In a recent development, local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

In a recent development, together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

According to recent reports, this release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie indicates reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:.

Industry observers note that source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Industry observers note that open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:.

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Recent findings suggest that voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:.

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.
